# Forecast for the next 48 hours

For this assignment, I selected Dublin as the target location and extracted the data from the "Forecast for the next 48 hours" table as my name is "Despoina". The scraped information was then structured into a clean table format, excluding weather symbols and preserving all relevant data fields.

```{r, include=FALSE}
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(httr)
```

## The original table from the site

![Forecast for the next 48 hours](Desktop/Screenshot%202026-03-27%20at%2017.29.25.png){width="456"}

```{r}

```

## Export data and Clean the Table

In this step, I cleaned and restructured the scraped weather table for Dublin by combining day and period information into meaningful column headers. Additionally, I removed unnecessary rows to create a clear dataset suitable for further analysis.

```{r}
url <- "https://www.timeanddate.com/weather/ireland/dublin"

page <- GET(url, add_headers("Accept-Language" = "en-US"))


html <- read_html(httr::GET(url, httr::add_headers("Accept-Language" = "en")))


weather_table <- html %>%
  html_element("#wt-48") %>%
  html_table()
new_headers <- paste(colnames(weather_table), weather_table[1, ])
new_headers[1] <- "Category"
colnames(weather_table) <- new_headers # Apply the new combined names to the table

# Move the weather descriptions (Row 4) into the Forecast row (Row 2)
weather_table[2, 2:ncol(weather_table)] <- weather_table[4, 2:ncol(weather_table)]
weather_table[2, 1] <- "Forecast"

weather_table <- weather_table[-c(1, 4), ] # Remove rows 1 and 4
weather_table <- head(weather_table, -1)  # Remove the footer
```

## View the Forecast for the next 48 hours table

```{r, include=FALSE}

library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
```

```{r}
kbl(weather_table,
    booktabs = TRUE,
    caption = "Detailed Weather Forecast Analysis",
    align = "lccccccc") %>%
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "scale_down", "hold_position"),
    full_width = FALSE
  ) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, color = "white", background = "#4472c4") %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, border_right = TRUE)
```

# Detailed Hourly Forecast

For this task, I extracted data from the "Detailed Hourly Forecast Next 24 hours" for Dublin and visualised the predicted trends of temperature, wind, and humidity, with properly formatted date and time values.

```{r}


url <- "https://www.timeanddate.com/weather/ireland/dublin/hourly"

# Fetch data
html <- read_html(httr::GET(url, httr::add_headers("Accept-Language" = "en")))

# cleaning
hourly_table <- html %>%
  html_table() %>%
  .[[1]]

# Handle Headers
colnames(hourly_table) <- hourly_table[1, ]
hourly_table <- hourly_table[-c(1, 2), ] # Remove the header and "Comfort" row
hourly_table <- head(hourly_table, -1)   # Remove the footer

# Remove the 2nd column,keep only the specific columns we want
hourly_table <- hourly_table %>%
  select(Time, Temp, Wind, Humidity)

# Final filter to remove empty time rows
hourly_table <- hourly_table[hourly_table$Time != "", ]
```

## View the Hourly Forecast table

```{r}
# We use 'scale_down' here because you want it to fit the page width perfectly
kbl(hourly_table,
    booktabs = TRUE,
    caption = "Hourly Forecast (Dublin)",
    align = "lccc") %>%
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "scale_down", "hold_position"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    font_size = 8 # Smaller font helps fit more rows on one page
  ) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, color = "white", background = "#4472c4") %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, border_right = TRUE)
```

## Hourly Weather Forecast Plot

In the following, we can see the plots created for Dublin, displayed one below the other, illustrating the hourly development of humidity, temperature, and wind over the next 24 hours.

```{r, include=FALSE}

library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

```

```{r,}
# Clean data and shorten Time labels
plot_data <- hourly_table %>%
  mutate(
    # Keep only the first two digits of the Time
    Time_Short = stringr::str_extract(Time, "^\\d{2}"),

    # Convert weather strings to pure numbers
    Temp = as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9\\-]", "", Temp)),
    Wind = as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9]", "", Wind)),
    Humidity = as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9]", "", Humidity)),

    # Keep the original order of the website
    Order = row_number()
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Temp, Wind, Humidity),
               names_to = "Condition",
               values_to = "Value")

# Create the plot
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = reorder(Time_Short, Order), y = Value, fill = Condition)) +
  geom_area(aes(group = Condition), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(group = Condition), color = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~Condition, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  # Custom colors: Red for Temp, Blue for Humidity, Grey for Wind
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Temp" = "purple",
                               "Humidity" = "#377eb8",
                               "Wind" = "#008080")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Hourly Weather Forecast: Dublin",
    x = "Hour of Day",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  )

```

# Annual Weather Averages

For this task, I retrieved the monthly annual weather averages from the "Climate (Averages) - Annual Weather Averages" table for Dublin by extracting the data directly from the climate table object and structuring it into a clean format. Use the html_node in order to take all the tables from the div.

```{r, include=FALSE}
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(kableExtra)
library(stringr)
```

```{r}
url <- "https://www.timeanddate.com/weather/ireland/dublin/climate"

html <- GET(url, add_headers("Accept-Language" = "en")) %>%
  read_html()



climate <- html %>% html_node("#climateTable")

months <- climate %>% html_nodes(".climate-month")

#months[[1]]

data_list <- lapply(months, function(m) {

  title <- m %>% html_node("h3") %>% html_text(trim = TRUE)

  values <- m %>% html_nodes("p") %>% html_text(trim = TRUE)

  # Extract numbers
  max_temp <- str_extract(values[1], "\\d+")
  min_temp  <- str_extract(values[2], "\\d+")
  mean_temp <- str_extract(values[3], "\\d+")
  precip    <- str_extract(values[4], "\\d+\\.?\\d*")

  data.frame(
    Month = title,
    Maximum = as.numeric(max_temp),
    Minimum = as.numeric(min_temp),
    Mean = as.numeric(mean_temp),
    Precipitation = as.numeric(precip)
  )
})

climate_df <- do.call(rbind, data_list)
# Remove the repetitive suffix from the Month column
climate_df$Month <- str_remove(climate_df$Month, " Climate & Weather Averages in Dublin")
```

## View Annual Weather Averages table

```{r}
kbl(climate_df,
    booktabs = TRUE,
    caption = "Dublin Monthly Climate Averages",
    align = "lcccc") %>%
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    font_size = 10
  ) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, color = "white", background = "#4472c4") %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, border_right = TRUE)

```

## Monthly Climate Overview Plot

In the following, we can see the plot created for Dublin, where the shaded area represents monthly precipitation levels, while the line and error bars illustrate the average temperature and its minimum–maximum range throughout the year.

```{r}

# Clean data: Remove "All Year"
plot_df <- climate_df[climate_df$Month != "All Year", ]
plot_df$Month <- factor(plot_df$Month, levels = month.name)

#  Create the plot
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = Month)) +
  # Use group = 1 to ensure the area connects across the x-axis factors
  geom_area(aes(y = Precipitation, fill = "Precipitation (mm)", group = 1),
            alpha = 0.4) +

  # ERROR BARS
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Minimum * 4, ymax = Maximum * 4, color =
                      "Temp Range (Min/Max)"),
                width = 0.3, size = 0.8) +

  # Mean Temperature
  geom_line(aes(y = Mean * 4, color = "Mean Temperature (°C)", group = 1), size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Mean * 4, color = "Mean Temperature (°C)"), size = 3) +

  # Set the two Y-axes scales
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Precipitation (mm)",
    limits = c(0, 100), # Adjusted to fit the scaled Max temp (20*4 = 80)
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~./4, name = "Temperature (°C)")
  ) +

  # Define colors
  scale_fill_manual(name = "", values = c("Precipitation (mm)" = "purple")) +
  scale_color_manual(name = "",
                     values = c("Mean Temperature (°C)" = "red",
                                "Temp Range (Min/Max)" = "darkred")) +

  # Final styling
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Dublin Monthly Climate Overview",
       subtitle = "Area represents Precipitation and  Error bars show Temp Range",
       x = "Month") +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```
